studentRecords.vocab:
Landside

The public areas of an airport terminal (ticketing, check-in, arrivals hall) accessible without a boarding pass.


Self-Service Kiosk

Automated touchscreens where passengers check in, print boarding passes, and generate baggage tags independently.


Automated Bag Drop

A conveyor system where ticketed travelers scan luggage tags and deposit checked bags without agent help.


Security Screening Checkpoint

The inspection point using metal detectors, body scanners, and X-ray machines to examine carry-on luggage.


Airside

The secure airport zone beyond security, including departure lounges, duty-free retail, gates, and aircraft stands.


Dwell Time

The duration passengers spend in the terminal between clearing security and boarding, driving retail revenue.


Boarding Gate

The concourse doorway and service counter through which ticketed travelers present passes to board.


Jet Bridge (Airbridge)

An enclosed, movable telescopic bridge linking the airport departure gate directly to the airplane door.


Apron (Ramp)

The designated paved area where aircraft park to load passengers, refuel, load baggage, and undergo servicing.


Movement Area

The aerodrome surface comprising runways, taxiways, and aprons used for aircraft surface movement.


Manoeuvring Area

The runways and taxiways strictly managed for aircraft surface movements, distinct from terminal servicing aprons.


Pushback Tug

A specialized heavy vehicle used to push aircraft backward out of their parking stands into taxi lanes.


Marshaller

Ground handling personnel using illuminated wands to guide pilots precisely into an apron parking stand.


Foreign Object Debris (FOD)

Loose items, trash, or metal fragments on taxiways or runways capable of damaging aircraft engines or tires.


Taxiway Centerline

A solid yellow line painted on taxiway pavement that pilots align with nose gear to ensure wingtip obstacle clearance.


Runway-Holding Position

A mandatory painted marking (two solid and two dashed yellow lines) and red sign where aircraft must stop short.


Runway Incursion

Any unauthorized presence of an aircraft, vehicle, or pedestrian on a protected runway surface designated for takeoff or landing.


Runway Designator (Numbering)

The two-digit number painted on a runway end representing its magnetic azimuth rounded to the nearest 10 degrees.


Hold Short Line

A painted line before a runway where aircraft and vehicles must stop until cleared by air traffic control.


Taxiway Guideline Lighting

Green lights embedded along the center of a taxiway to guide pilots safely during night operations or low visibility.


Stop Bar

A row of flush red lights across a taxiway pavement that warns vehicles and pilots not to enter an active runway.


Apron Taxi Lane

A designated route on the apron designed to allow aircraft access to and from parking stands.


Follow-Me Car

A marked airport vehicle with flashing yellow lights that guides aircraft to their parking stand in low visibility.


Baggage Conveyor Belt

A moving belt system that carries checked luggage from the check-in hall to the baggage sorting area.


Body Scanner

A security screening device using millimeter-waves to detect hidden objects without physical contact.


Biometric E-Gate

An automated border or boarding gate using facial recognition cameras to verify a traveler's identity.


Passengers with Reduced Mobility (PRM)

Travelers who need dedicated assistance through the airport due to physical disability, age, or medical condition.


Flight Information Display System (FIDS)

Electronic screens throughout the terminal showing real-time departure, arrival, and gate information.


Service Road

Marked roadways on the airfield reserved strictly for ground handling vehicles, fuel trucks, and baggage tugs.


Blast Fence

A physical barrier placed on the airfield to protect ground vehicles, people, and buildings from aircraft jet engine blast.

Modal Shift

Encouraging travelers or cargo to switch from high-carbon transport (like cars or planes) to greener options (like trains or buses).


High-Speed Rail (HSR)

Electrified passenger trains operating over 250 km/h, providing a low-carbon competitor to domestic flights.


Life-Cycle Emissions

The total greenhouse gas emissions generated throughout vehicle manufacturing, operation, maintenance, and disposal.


Territorial Equity

Ensuring that rural and remote areas have fair access to reliable, affordable public transport—not just big cities.


Intermodal Hub

A transit node seamlessly integrating rail, metro, bus, shared mobility, and pedestrian corridors.


Decarbonization

The process of eliminating carbon dioxide emissions from transportation fuels and propulsion systems.


Electrification

Converting transit lines from fossil fuels to electric power supplied by renewable grids.


Active Mobility

Human-powered travel modes, primarily cycling and walking, producing zero operational emissions.


Corridor Capacity

The maximum passenger or freight volume that a transit route can transport within a given timeframe.


Fleet Modernization

Systematic replacement of aging vehicles with energy-efficient, low-emission models.


Containerisation

The standardized shipping container system developed in the late 20th century that transformed global trade.


Point-to-Point Transit

A network architecture where vehicles travel directly between origin and destination without intermediate hubs.


Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF)

Non-petroleum-based drop-in aviation fuel derived from waste oils, agricultural residues, or captured carbon.


Traffic Congestion

Gridlock conditions when traffic volume exceeds roadway capacity, causing delays and excess idling emissions.


Micro-Mobility

Small, lightweight transportation devices operating at low speeds, such as e-scooters and e-bikes.


Induced Demand

The phenomenon where increasing roadway capacity results in increased vehicular traffic rather than congestion relief.


Modal Split

The percentage of total passenger journeys completed using each transport mode within a given region.


Low-Emission Zone (LEZ)

A designated geographic area where access by polluting vehicles is restricted or subject to penalty fees.


Night Train (Sleeper Train)

Long-distance passenger trains operating overnight with sleeping berths, offering a low-carbon alternative to domestic flights.


Door-to-Door Travel Time

The total time required for a complete journey, from leaving home or the office until arriving at the final destination.


Carpooling

Sharing car journeys with other travelers going to the same destination to reduce travel costs, fuel consumption, and road traffic.


Public Transit Subsidy

Financial assistance provided by governments to keep bus, metro, and train fares affordable for citizens.


Cycling Infrastructure

Protected bike lanes, secure parking stations, and bike-sharing networks designed to support safe everyday bicycle travel.


Grid Capacity

The maximum amount of electrical power that a regional power network can transmit to charge electric vehicles and trains.


Congestion Charge

A fee charged to drivers entering city centers during peak hours to encourage walking, cycling, or public transport.


Short-Haul Flight

A commercial flight typically covering under 500 to 800 kilometers that can often be replaced by high-speed rail connections.


Transit-Oriented Development

Urban planning that clusters housing, shops, and offices within easy walking distance of major rail and transit stations.


First-Mile / Last-Mile Transit

The first or final leg of a commuter's journey between home or work and a public transport hub.


Shared Mobility

Transportation services and vehicles (like rental bikes, scooters, and carsharing fleets) shared among users on demand.


Carbon Intensity

The amount of carbon dioxide emitted per passenger-kilometer or per ton of freight moved across a transport network.

studentRecords.vocab:
We got to learn the difference between mostly used professional terms that could be easily mixed up each others.

The difference between LANDSIDE and AIRSIDE. The landside is the first area we got to walk in while entering an airport. It is accessible to anyone. The airside is the secured operational area beyond the security checkpoint. It includes all the different areas of the airport that are beyond the security gate. 

the difference between AIRLINE and AERODROME OPERATOR. The airline owns the aircrafts and provide commercial passenger and cargo air transports. The aerodrome operator owns the airport infrastructure in itself and enable airlines to provide flights services to their customers.

The difference between SCHEDULED FLIGHT and CHARTER FLIGHT. A scheduled flight is fixed and provided regardless of passenger load while a charter flight is one flight booked by a specific organization for a specific slot of time.

The distinction between a DELAY and a FLIGHT CANCELLATION. A delay means that the flight will still be provided but within a different slot time from the originally scheduled one. A flight cancellation means that the flight has been called off. In this situation the passengers will either be allocated to alternative flights or fully refund with statutory compensations.

We also got to learn some abbreviations. 
AODB for Airport Operational DataBase (that manages flight schedules, stand allocations and gate changes)
TRC for Turnaround Coordinator (the airside manager who supervises all ground activities between arrival and departure)
GPU for Ground Power Unit (a mobile generator that provides electricity and air conditioning to the aircraft with engines and APU off)
GSE for Ground Support Equipment (all mobile ground equipment that ensure ground manoeuvre)

studentRecords.content:
Today's lesson theme was about the evolution of public transportation. 
We could first get engaged in the course through a drawing game where we had to make the members of our team guess the animal we were drawing soon the whiteboard. 

Then, we could individually participate to another game whose aim was to recap all the vocabulary learnt in the previous lesson. We could steal point to our classmates which created a fierce commitment within us. The looser had to be devoured by the dragon. 

the following activity was in pair working and we could discuss the benefits and downsides of each great period of transportation that are the 4 following ones : the STEAM RAILWAY (1950-70's) that produced a lot of local smoke and a massive carbon dioxyde amount as the coal fired powered trains were not green.  The POST WAR JET and AUTOMOBILE BOOM (1950-70's) that generated a significant carbon dioxyde emission on the rise and was highly dependent to oil consumption. The CONTAINERIZATION ERA (1980-2010's) that shaped the globalized supply chain. The current period that is an electrification of means of transportation era as well as a SAF using era on talks because SAF (Sustainable Aviation Fuels) are not used that much currently and they are highly carbon dioxyde generating for their production. 

Then, still in pair working, we could debate the wiser mean of transportation to get to Paris from Toulouse. W could choose either the plane or the. train. Admitedly, the train is a free carbon dioxyde emitting mean of transportation but the plane is faster and less expensive. However, we could all the same underline that sometimes the train is more spacious and it's also more convenient when arriving to the final destination because the station is directly integrated to the city. 

finally, we could work on 3 ways to pollute less 
- using high speed rails rather than flying because it is a carbon free alternative for domestic journeys. 
- work from home and fund an association with the money it makes us save. 
- promoting a car-sharing network rather than being selfish in our own old heavily polluting car

and 2 ways to promote greener travel habits as regards ENAC inner organization. A lot of ideas emerged but some of the most striking ones were :
- being deducted directly from our salary the amount of flight ticket we could purchase (so that we pay twice). 
- renting electric vehicles from a car-sharing network rather than driving our own polluting ones.

The distance of a flight will makes us describe it as SHORT, MEDIUM or LONG HAUL. 

finally we could make a differentiation between a CONVEYER BELT and a CAROUSEL and also between SAFETY (describe protection from unintentional harm) and SECURITY (describe protection against intentional harm).

We could discuss some new vocabulary in pair working. LANDSIDE CHECK IN and BAG DROP are both part of a procedure when people can print themselves their boarding pass and baggage tags inside the airport and then deposit their luggage at an automated conveyer. 

SECURITY SCREENING CHECKPOINT is when luggage go through X-rays while passengers walk through metal detectors or body scanners. 

AIRSIDE CONCOURSE is an inner area in the airside where people can walk along while intending to board an airplane. 

DWELL TIME is a time people wait between arriving from a flight and departing for the next one. 

The BOARDING GATE is a check in point that people must go through before boarding a plane walking across the JET BRIDGE.

studentRecords.vocab:
Today is a holiday so we could work on the session independently. We could mobilize a work environment vocabulary and training to define it using grammar structures such as USED FOR + ING or DESIGNED TO + BV along with the use of THAT or WHICH. 

In this way, I could describe some airside specialized vehicles. 
The PUSHBACK TUG is a vehicle designed to get the aircraft out of its parking area. It can be a tower or a towbarless tractor that basically enable the aircraft not to waste its fuel for ground manoeuvring and prevent aircraft from making noisy apron atmosphere. 

The GROUND POWER UNIT is a mobile vehicule that provides electricity power to the parked aircraft with all engines off. It is used for maintaining the aircraft operative while standing in the boarding gate. 

The POTABLE WATER TRUCK is designed to provide clear water to the aircraft which is essential for ensuring a comfortable flight with refreshment commodities. 

The LAVORATORY SERVICE TRUCK is used by the hygienic team to carry all the sanitary equipment to clean the cabin. It is used for everyday cleaning service. 

The DE-ICING TRUCK is designed to remove ice from the aircraft which is essential for flying performance and the efficiency of flying measurement instruments. 

The FOLLOW ME CAR is used for leading aircraft to the apron area on bad weather conditions. Using flashy yellow lights, it is easily recognizable for the flight crew. 

Then, we could express cause and consequence using grammar structures such as DUE TO - OWING TO - AS A RESULT OF - LED TO - CONSEQUENTLY. 

here are a few examples of sentences we could make. 

- Due to late passengers, the aircraft was waiting in the ramp a little longer. 
- Some troubles at the boarding gate could lead to delays owing to passengers inconsistent documentations or seat disputes. 
- Some passengers couldn't board as a result of overbooking issues which led to delays because the flight crew had to deal with a storm of protest. 
- Heavy snow fall has been reported and consequently it created some delays because aircraft were unable to takeoff on a scheduled time. 

We could also express operational conditions with a structured sentence based on the use of IF and WILL/MUST. 

- If the passenger cannot provide a consistent boarding pass they must not smoothly board the aircraft.
- If the refueler truck is late the plane will not be able to takeoff on a scheduled time.

here is an example of report : " Aircraft F-G22O boarding in progress. estimated 15 delay due to an inconsistent boarding pass. The fuel tanker is late leading to another estimated delay of 30 minutes. Could you please use de-escalation to calm passengers down. Another unforeseeable events may occur so the estimated time of departure hasn't been fixed yet. "

These are my answers to the questions that were asked (as we could not do it in class) : 
If catering arrives 5 minutes late, why does it cascade into a 20-minute slot loss ?
A five-minute catering delay usually turns into a much longer twenty-minute wait because airplanes must stick to strict departure slots. ATC gives every flight a specific departure time window and if the catering truck finishes late, the cabin crew cannot shut the doors on time, which causes the plane to miss its assigned takeoff spot. Once that initial slot is lost, the plane goes back in line, and controllers must find a new place in the busy runway traffic to clear for departure that said flight. 
What's new this week in aviation ?
Aviation headlines this week focus have focused on how airlines and airports use digital tools to reduce flight delays. There are also global organizations like ICAO and IATA pushing for better air traffic management systems to keep planes moving smoothly and to gain efficiency. Moreover, many airlines are dealing with plane shortages because new aircraft deliveries are delayed across the industry. Due to strict environmental rules, airports are also looking for clever ways to handle more passengers without building new runways and therefore polluting more.

studentRecords.vocab:
We learnt a lot of vocabulary today :
- push-back tug : the vehicle which push the aircraft outside the parking stand. It's also known as a tug.
- jet bridge : a telescopic bridge linking the airport (the boarding gate) to the aircraft (the airplane door). It's mainly used for big airplanes while we use moving stairs for the others.
- apron/ramp : the parking area where the aircraft wait during the turnaround time. It's located in the airside.
- windsock : fabric tube which shows both the direction and the speed of the wind. This is essential for any aerodrome in the world.
- duty free : buying something without paying local or national import duties. This is common in the international transit areas such as airports.
- dwell time : the time passengers spend in the terminal (security and boarding check-in...). New technologies like bio-metric e-gate, facial recognition and automated bag drop are useful to reduce this time.
- automated bag drop : a way to register and drop your luggage by yourself  
- runway-holding position : a specific place (a big line on the floor) where the aircraft has to stop and wait for instructions. This is like a border between the taxiway and the runway.
- baggage conveyor belt : moving track which transports checked luggage automatically between different points in the airport. It's also known as a baggage carousel.

studentRecords.vocab:
- short-haul flight : a flight which covers short distances (between 500 and 800 km) and can be replaced by rail connections. This was a dilemma during the debates because the flight is faster and cheaper than train but its carbon footprint is huge compared to high-speed rail connections.
- cycling infrastructure : it refers to all the infrastructures dedicated to people who use bikes in cities. It can be bike lanes, secured parking etc.
- shared mobility : act of sharing transportation services and vehicles with other users to reduce their individual carbon footprint. Carpooling is an example of shared mobility and can be used to go to the airport.
- door-to-door travel time : total time required for a complete journey, between your house and your final destination for example. This time can be quit long for a flight because you spend a lot of time at the airport to complete all the security check-points.
- night train : a rail connection which departs in the evening and arrives later in the night or in the morning. There are sleeping berths inside these trains. It can be a good alternative to short-haul flights.
- micro mobility : it refers to small and slow vehicles such as bikes, scooters (electric or not). It is really useful and efficient for short routes because it doesn't pollutes.
- Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) : a new type of fuel made with waste oils and plants. It is already used by some airlines but it is still more expensive than usual fuel and the retrofit for the engines is sometimes complicated.
- fleet modernization : act of replacing old vehicles by more efficient and low-emission ones. Some people want the aircraft to be removed from service when they fly since at least 15 years but this idea is really appreciate.
- active mobility : human-powered travel modes like walking and cycling. It remains the best way to reduce our daily carbon footprint (by biking to work for example).
- electrification : the act of converting public transportation and other vehicles to an electric propulsion (buses in Toulouse for example)
- High-speed rail : electrified passenger trains which operates over 250 km/h. This is, with night trains, a good alternative to short-haul flights.

studentRecords.vocab:
The vocabulary in this session was mainly focused on the Ground Support Equipment :
- chocks-on/chocks-off : Chocks are wedges placed against aircraft landing wheels to prevent the aircraft from moving while parked at the apron. They are installed after arrival (Chocks-On) and removed before departure (Chocks-Off), when authorized.
- Pushback Tug : specialized vehicle used to push an aircraft backwards from its parking stand. It is also known as a tractor.
- GPU : external power source that supplies electricity to an aircraft while its engines are switched off. It is used during aircraft parking and turnaround time to power onboard systems such as light and ventilation.
- Belt loader : mobile conveyor belt used to load and unload baggage and cargo from the aircraft hold. It is used during baggage handling operations.
- Hydrant dispenser : vehicle that transfers fuel from the airport's underground hydrant system to the aircraft. It is used during aircraft refueling at airports equipped with a hydrant network.
- Catering hi-lift truck : specialized vehicle with an elevated platform used to deliver food and beverages to an aircraft. It is used during catering operations to load and unload meal carts through the aircraft cabin door.
- Potable water truck : specialized vehicle that supplies fresh drinking water to the aircraft. It is used during ground servicing to refill the aircraft's water tanks.
- Lavatory service unit : vehicle used to empty and service aircraft toilet waste tanks. It is used during aircraft turnaround to remove waste and replenish the lavatory servicing system as required.
- De-icing/anti-icing rig : specialized vehicle that sprays fluids onto aircraft surfaces to remove ice and protect against further ice accumulation. It is used in cold weather conditions before departure when icing or frost is present or expected.
- Follow-Me car : high-visibility airport vehicle used to guide aircraft on the airport movement area. It is used when an aircraft needs assistance following an authorized taxi route to its assigned stand or another location.
- Baggage tug and dolly train : small towing vehicle pulling several baggage carts. It is used to transport luggage between the terminal, baggage handling area and aircraft stand.
- CTOT : stands for Calculated Take-Off Time, which is the assigned take-off time for a flight subject to air traffic flow management restrictions.
- Stand clearance : confirmation that the aircraft parking stand is clear of personnel and equipment as required for a safe departure. It is confirmed before pushback to make sure that the aircraft can leave its stand safely.
There are also some other words that we had already learnt like Turnaround Time.
studentRecords.content: In this session we learnt more about the ground operations, especially during the turnaround time. It was the occasion to learn a lot of vocabulary to describe many Ground Support Equipment (pushback tug, potable water and lavatory service truck...), but also to understand how the time is managed during these operations. We also discovered how to explain briefly and clearly causes and consequences when there is a problem during the ground operations. Furthermore we saw the four steps of the briefing : Identification, Operational Status, Root cause and delay, Action and revised Estimated Time of Departure.

topBuzzwords.definition: Landside = public areas before security (check-in, arrivals hall). Airside = strictly secured operations areas beyond security (gates, apron, taxiways, runways).
The designated paved area where aircraft park at designated stands to board/deboard, refuel, load baggage, and undergo ground servicing.
Essential communicative collocations: to book a flight, to board a plane, to check in, to clear customs, and to travel with carry-on luggage.
GPU (Ground Power Unit) = mobile ground generator supplying electricity at the gate. APU (Auxiliary Power Unit) = small gas turbine in the aircraft tail used when engines and GPU are off.

topBuzzwords.definition: Conversational storytelling idioms: to hit the road (depart), to take the scenic route (longer picturesque path), and to be in the driver's seat (in control).

Scheduled = timetabled regular airline service. Charter = booked on-demand for a specific private/tour group. Severe delays trigger passenger statutory care.

grammarTrapsCaught.title: ❌ 'Luggages' and 'Trainings' do NOT exist!
grammarTrapsCaught.rule: Both 'luggage' and 'training' are uncountable nouns in English. Never add an 's'.
grammarTrapsCaught.correctExample: ✅ "We checked three pieces of luggage and completed our training course."

grammarTrapsCaught.title: 🗣️ Pronunciation Trap: Itinerary
grammarTrapsCaught.rule: Multiple students flagged pronunciation difficulty with 'itinerary'. Stress is on the second syllable: /aɪˈtɪn.ər.ər.i/ (eye-TIN-er-uh-ree).
grammarTrapsCaught.correctExample: ✅ "Could you please confirm our flight itinerary before we head to the gate?"

grammarTrapsCaught.title: ⏱️ Reported Speech Backshift & Time References
grammarTrapsCaught.rule: When reporting past dialogue, tenses shift back (present -> past, past -> past perfect; will -> would), and time adverbs shift ('today' -> 'that day', 'yesterday' -> 'the day before', 'tomorrow' -> 'the following day').
grammarTrapsCaught.correctExample: ✅ "He said he was running on empty that day and would take the train the following morning."

grammarTrapsCaught.title: 📍 Preposition Trap: At vs. In vs. Into
grammarTrapsCaught.rule: Watch out for spatial prepositions: use 'at' for a specific point/facility (at the airport, at the gate), 'in' for an enclosed space (in the cabin), and 'into' for direction/movement (boarded into the aircraft).
grammarTrapsCaught.correctExample: ✅ "We arrived at Toulouse-Blagnac Airport, waited at gate 12, and boarded into the aircraft."

grammarTrapsCaught.title: ✈️ Apron vs. Taxiway vs. Runway
grammarTrapsCaught.rule: Exact spatial precision is required in operational briefings. Never refer to the runway when you mean parking on the apron or taxiing on taxiway Alpha.
grammarTrapsCaught.correctExample: ✅ "The aircraft pushed back from stand B4 onto the apron, taxied via Charlie, and lined up on Runway 14L."

grammarTrapsCaught.title: 💡 'Used to do' vs. 'Be used to doing'
grammarTrapsCaught.rule: 'I used to work' expresses a past habit that is finished. 'I am used to working' means you are accustomed/familiar with it now.
grammarTrapsCaught.correctExample: ✅ "I used to live in Paris, but now I am used to living in Toulouse."
